terms.gloss: an eclipse (“a failing”), with sōlis or lūnae
evidence: Cic. Div. 2.17: Sōlis dēfectiōnēs itemque lūnae praedīcuntur in multōs annōs
terms.comment: Cicero’s word. The verb is dēficere: sōl dēficit, the sun is eclipsed (Cic. Rep. 1.25, below).

evidence: Lucr. 5.751: Sōlis item quoque dēfectūs lūnaeque latebrās

terms.comment: The Greek word, used by the Rhetorica ad Herennium and Pliny; Lewis & Short calls dēfectiō and dēfectus the pure Latin.

phrases.latin: Hodiē sōl dēficiet; nōlī eum intuērī.
phrases.english: There’s an eclipse of the sun today; don’t look straight at it.

phrases.latin: erat enim tum haec nova et ignōta ratiō, sōlem lūnae oppositū solēre dēficere
phrases.english: for this explanation was new and unknown then: that the sun is eclipsed when the moon gets in its way

phrases.latin: Sōlis dēfectiōnēs itemque lūnae praedīcuntur in multōs annōs ab iīs quī sīderum mōtūs numerīs persequuntur
phrases.english: eclipses of the sun, and of the moon too, are foretold many years ahead by those who follow the movements of the stars with calculations

sources: Lewis & Short: defectio · Lewis & Short: defectus · Lewis & Short: eclipsis
